title: Ser or estar?
topic: ser and estar: identity, origin, character / state, location, result
why: After ser, tener and reflexive verbs, here's estar, the second "to be" that English doesn't have. The lesson gives simple guidelines (what you are / where and how you are) and the adjective pairs that change meaning, so you avoid the most common mistakes from the very start.

Estar: the second \"to be\"

English has only one verb \"to be\". Spanish has two: ser, which you know, and estar. It's the big challenge of Spanish for an English speaker… but with a few simple guidelines, you'll choose correctly almost every time.

serestar
yosoyestoy
túeresestás
él, ella, ustedesestá
nosotros, nosotrassomosestamos
vosotros, vosotrassoisestáis
ellos, ellas, ustedessonestán

Look at the accents in estar: every form has one, except estoy and estamos. The stress falls on the last syllable: es-tás, es-tá, es-tán.

Watch the accent on está: está (he is, she is) and esta (this) are two different words. ¿Dónde está? = Where is it? Always write the accent.

The simplest question: ¿Cómo estás?

You'll hear it everywhere. It asks how you are right now: that's a state, so it takes estar.

—¿Cómo estás? —Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?—How are you? —I'm fine, thanks. And you?
—¿Cómo está usted? —Muy bien, gracias.—How are you? (formal) —Very well, thank you.

Take Muy bien (very well) as a set phrase: the word muy (very) will be covered in an upcoming lesson.

Don't mix up ¿Cómo estás? (how are you?) and ¿Cómo eres? (what are you like? what's your personality?): ¿Cómo es Ana? — Es simpática.

Bien (well, fine) and mal (bad, unwell) always go with estar: Estoy bien, Estoy mal. Never \"soy bien\".

", "

Ser or estar: the guidelines

Ser says what you are: what defines a person or a thing. Estar says where you are and how you are right now.

SER: what you areExamples
identitySoy Pablo. Es la hermana de Lucía.
nationality, originSomos franceses. Es de Bilbao.
professionElena es enfermera.
personalityJavier es simpático y tranquilo.
materialLa mesa es de madera.
timeSon las tres. Es la una.
ESTAR: where and how you areExamples
locationEstoy en casa. ¿Dónde está el museo? Madrid está en España.
temporary stateEstoy cansado. Lucía está enferma.
moodEstamos contentos. Diego está enfadado.
how you're doing¿Cómo estás? Estoy bien.

The test for choosing

  • Am I saying who or what (name, job, origin, personality)? → ser.
  • Am I saying where? → estar. Even for a city or a country, which never move: Sevilla está en Andalucía.
  • Am I saying how I feel right now? → estar: Hoy estoy cansada.
Soy francés, pero estoy en Madrid.I'm French, but I'm in Madrid.
Carmen es simpática, pero hoy está enfadada.Carmen is nice, but today she's angry.

Unlike English, adjectives agree with the person, like nationalities: Pablo está cansado, Lucía está cansada, estamos cansados. So a woman says Estoy cansada, a man Estoy cansado.

", "

Same adjective, different meaning

Some adjectives change meaning depending on the verb. With ser, it's the nature of the person or thing; with estar, it's a state of the moment.

Adjectivewith SERwith ESTAR
aburridoEs aburrido: he's boring.Está aburrido: he's bored.
listoEs listo: he's smart, clever.Está listo: he's ready.
maloEs malo: he's bad, mean.Está malo: he's sick.
ricoEs rico: he's rich.Está rico: it's delicious.
La película es aburrida y estoy aburrido.The movie is boring and I'm bored.
—¿Estás lista? —¡Sí, estoy lista!—Are you ready? —Yes, I'm ready!
¡La tortilla está rica!The omelet is delicious!

With the time and reflexive verbs

The time always takes ser, and now you can describe how you feel during the day:

Son las siete. Me levanto, pero estoy cansado.It's seven o'clock. I get up, but I'm tired.
Me acuesto a las doce porque estoy nervioso.I go to bed at midnight because I'm nervous.

Learn the first two pairs by heart: \"boring / bored\" and \"smart / ready\". English speakers often say soy aburrido for \"I'm bored\"… and end up saying they're a boring person!
